summary: Describes a method for making random selections so that the unbiased nature of the choice can be publicly verified, such as for choosing nominating committee members. This is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 3797.

eli5.summary: It is a fair way to draw names from a hat where everybody can check that the draw was not rigged.

questions: how to make a publicly verifiable random selection
how does the ietf select committee members
how to combine multiple random sources
subtitle: A fair, publicly verifiable way to select committee members at random.

tldr.problem: Selecting committee members at random requires trust that the selection was not rigged or biased in favor of any candidate.
tldr.mechanism: Announce the algorithm and future sources of randomness (like lottery results) in advance, then apply a cryptographic hash function to combine those sources and select members, allowing anyone to verify the fairness.
tldr.outcome: The IETF adopted this method for selecting its Nominating Committee, ensuring transparency and ending historical selection methods that relied on clergy or chance.

today: RFC 3797 replaced this RFC, refining the method further. The approach of publicly verifiable random selection remains the standard for IETF committee selection.

sections.title: The Committee Selection Problem
sections.content:
The IETF Nominations Committee (NomCom) selects members of the Internet Engineering Steering Group and the Internet Architecture Board. Each year, volunteers are solicited and 10 of them are randomly chosen as voting members.

The challenge is that the selection must appear unbiased to the entire community. If one person makes the selection in secret, their fairness will always be questioned, even if they acted honestly. The solution is to make the selection transparent and reproducible: announce the algorithm and the random seed in advance, then let anyone verify the math.
sections.eli5: When you pick people for a team, everyone wants to know the choice was fair. One way to prove fairness is to let everyone see the random numbers you used and the math you did.

sections.title: The Three-Step Process
sections.content:
The method has three phases. First, the list of eligible volunteers is published, giving the community a week or two to dispute who should be included. Second, the exact algorithm is announced along with the future sources of randomness (for example, specific lottery drawings that have not yet happened). Third, once those random events occur, their results are published, the selection algorithm is executed, and anyone can verify the results.

This ensures no one could have cheated: the algorithm was fixed before the random sources became known, so no one could have chosen the random sources to favor their preferred candidates.
sections.eli5: First, you publish the list of people to choose from. Then you say which lottery drawing you will use for randomness. Last, you run the lottery and do the math, so everyone can check you did it right.

sections.title: Sources of Randomness
sections.content:
Good randomness sources include government lottery drawings, stock closing prices, or sporting event results. The RFC recommends about three sources, with the most entropy coming from the final source (like a major lottery drawing) so that if someone had limited influence over an earlier source, they could not bias the result.

The algorithm combines these sources into a single string (for example, concatenating lottery numbers and stock prices), then runs the MD5 hash function repeatedly to generate the selection. MD5 produces 128 bits of output; the RFC notes that 40 bits of entropy is sufficient even for large volunteer pools.
sections.eli5: Pick random numbers from the real world, like lottery drawings or stock prices that nobody can control. Mix them together with math (a hash function) to decide who gets picked.

sections.title: Preventing Cheating
sections.content:
The security of this method rests on the principle that the administrator cannot know the random values when announcing the algorithm. If an administrator could influence the random sources after the algorithm is published, they might be able to bias the outcome. Therefore, the sources must be beyond anyone's control and truly public (like lottery drawings).

The RFC also notes that if a selected member must be replaced, new random sources must be announced for the replacement selection, avoiding any possibility that the original sources could be reused to manufacture a different outcome.
sections.eli5: The fairness comes from choosing your random numbers from things nobody can rig, like lottery drawings. You have to announce which lottery you will use before the lottery happens.
